title: KQL and SPL
summary: KQL, the Kusto Query Language, and SPL, the Splunk Search Processing Language, are the two query languages most commonly used by detection engineers and SOC analysts to interrogate security telemetry. Both are pipeline languages: a search begins with a source of events and a filter, then passes a tabular result through a chain of operators that project, extend, summarise, join, order and visualise. Their shared idioms matter more than their syntax. Progressive filtering keeps queries fast because the earliest stage should eliminate the most data. Time bounding is mandatory rather than optional, both for performance and because an unbounded query over a long retention window will time out or return misleading aggregates. Summarisation collapses many raw events into per-entity counts, which is how thresholds, rarity analysis and first-seen or last-seen logic are expressed. Joins between datasets such as endpoint process events and identity sign-in logs are what turn a weak single-source signal into a defensible detection. The differences are practical. KQL uses a pipe-forward style with tabular operators, has strong support for dynamic and JSON-typed columns, and is used across Microsoft security products and Azure services. SPL uses a search-command model with a large command library, is central to Splunk, and offers macros and lookups that many teams use to build reusable detection content. Fluency in either language is really fluency in a set of habits: knowing which fields carry trustworthy values, understanding how each platform handles timestamps and nulls, and testing query logic against deliberately constructed sample data before trusting it to raise alerts.
objectives: You will be able to read and construct pipeline-style queries that filter, project, extend, summarise and join security telemetry.
You will be able to translate a detection intent between KQL and SPL, accounting for differences in operator names and null handling.
You will be able to write threshold and rarity logic that uses summarisation rather than single-event triggers.
You will be able to join endpoint, identity and network datasets to corroborate a weak single-source signal.
You will be able to diagnose why a slow query is slow and restructure it for the platform's execution model.
You will be able to validate query logic against hand-built sample data before promoting it to a production detection.

beginner.definition: KQL and SPL are two query languages used to search security logs. KQL stands for Kusto Query Language. SPL stands for Splunk Search Processing Language. Both let you ask questions of huge amounts of log data and get a table of answers back.
beginner.whyItMatters: A security team collects millions of log lines every day. Reading them by hand is impossible. Query languages let you filter that flood down to the few events that matter. They are also how detection rules are written. If you cannot write a query, you cannot check whether a rule is correct.
howItWorks: You start with a data source, such as sign-in logs or process events from laptops.
You add a filter to keep only the rows you care about, such as one user.
You add another stage that counts events, groups them, or adds a new column.
Each stage passes its table result to the next stage, like water through pipes.
You finish with a sort and a limit so you see the most important rows first.
Before using a query as a detection, you run it against sample data you built yourself.
beginner.example: Picture a library with a million returned books piled in the hallway. You do not read every book. You ask a helper for books returned last week by one person, then sort them by title, then show only the first ten. Each request narrows the pile a little more. KQL and SPL queries work in that same step-by-step way. Each stage makes the pile smaller and more useful.
takeaways: Always limit your query to a time range before you run it.
Filter as early as possible so the search stays fast.
Test a query on sample data before turning it into a detection.
